sections.title: Full-body programs
sections.text: A full-body session trains several major movement patterns on the same day. Two or three days a week often works well for beginners and busy people. You practice the main exercises often without needing many gym visits. Sessions can get long if you include too many movements.

sections.title: Upper/lower programs
sections.text: An upper/lower plan alternates upper-body and lower-body sessions, often over four workouts a week. It leaves room for more exercises and sets, with recovery time between similar sessions. A three-day rotating version also works, and the calendar doesn’t have to repeat exactly every week.

sections.title: Muscle-group splits
sections.text: A body-part split might train chest and triceps one day, back and biceps another, and legs on a third. These programs make high training volumes easier to fit in. When the weekly work is similar, no split is better for muscle growth than another. A badly designed split can leave some muscles untrained for too long.

sections.title: Choose by your limits
sections.text: With two days, full-body is a practical default. With three, use full-body or a rotating upper/lower pattern. With four, use upper/lower or two different full-body days. Five days allow many arrangements, but extra visits add little if you can’t stick with them or recover from them. Skill practice and personal preference also play a part. Pick the simplest split that covers your goals, schedule and equipment, and keep an eye on your total weekly sets. A five-day schedule that looks advanced is not automatically better than a three-day plan you keep doing.
